item.title: Japan score in injury time to stun Brazil 3-2 in Singapore
item.description:
SOCCER-MIZUHOCUP-JPN-BRA/

Substitute Tatsuhiro Sakamoto netted his first international goal with a late winner as Japan edged Brazil 3-2 in a thrilling friendly at the National Stadium in Singapore on Saturday.

A brilliant brace by Vinicius Junior had erased a two-goal deficit after strikes by Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura put the Samurai Blue 2-0 up in the opening 19 minutes.

But Sakamoto was in the right place to fire home after latching on to Kodai Sano's deflected effort in stoppage time to give the Asian side a dramatic victory in front of 38,688 fans.

SAFF Championship: Bangladesh face Pakistan in semifinal today

In the first meeting between the teams since Brazil's 2-1 win in the round of 32 at the World Cup last June, the Samurai Blue seized the early initiative with two goals in a torrid four-minute spell.

On 15 minutes, a through ball by Ritsu Doan was picked up just inside the Brazilian half by Kubo who showed quick feet to cut inside Jair before firing a low effort past goalkeeper Pedro Morisco.

Japan added another shortly afterwards after some fine work by Shuto Nakano, who broke down the right flank and centred for an unmarked Nakamura to calmly place a right-footed shot into the bottom corner of the net.

Brazil responded with a magnificent goal by Vinicius in the 33rd minute.

Brazil beat India 4–0 in Kolkata friendly

Zion Suzuki had made an excellent stop to deny Estevao when he bore down on goal, but the Japan goalkeeper could do little when the ball fell to Vinicius who found the top corner with a right-footed diagonal drive.

Suzuki made good stops to deny Brazilian debutant Andre just before half-time and skipper Raphinha after the interval as Japan clung to their narrow lead.

But the Selecao were not to be denied and Vinicius put them back on level terms in the 75th minute with another fine finish as he cut in from the left flank and launched a low right-footed effort that found the net off the right post.

Brazil bask in festive welcome in Kolkata ahead of India friendly

Brazil went close to grabbing the winner as substitute Endrick rocked the crossbar with a fierce effort and Joao Gomes sent a low shot narrowly wide.

But in stoppage time, an effort by Kodai Sano took a fortunate bounce off a defender and fell nicely for Sakamoto to send the ball past Pedro Morisco.

Brazil appealed for a foul in the build-up to the goal but VAR upheld the goal and Raphinha was shown a red card for his vehement protests.

item.title: Case filed against Nusrat Tabassum's father over alleged land grabbing and house vandalism
item.description:
A case has been filed at Daulatpur Police Station in Kushtia against the father of Nusrat Tabassum, a member of parliament (MP) for the reserved women's seat and a leader of the National Citizen Party (NCP).

Nusrat’s father, Abdul Halim, has been accused of vandalising a residential house, assaulting its occupants, looting belongings and grabbing land.

The case was filed today, Saturday, by Idris Ali, 67, a resident of Bagoan Tension Mor area in Mathurapur union of Daulatpur upazila.

Abdul Halim is the sole named accused in the case, while eight to 10 unidentified people have also been accused.

Kushtia district police’s spokesperson, Additional Superintendent of Police Faisal Mahmud confirmed the case to Prothom Alo.

Speaking by phone at 6:00 pm on Saturday, he said a case has been filed against Abdul Halim. Sub-Inspector Mohsin Chowdhury of Daulatpur Police Station will investigate it.

Contacted about the case, Sub-Inspector Mohsin Chowdhury told Prothom Alo, “I have been assigned to investigate the case. That is all I know.”

Nusrat’s home fire: Heated exchanges in parliament over cause of blaze

What the case statement says

According to the case statement, Idris Ali bought four and a quarter kathas of land from two of Abdul Halim’s brothers about five years ago. After taking possession of the land, he built a house there and began living in it with his family.

Abdul Halim later planned to take forcible possession of the land. Against this backdrop, on the morning of 13 September last year, Abdul Halim and his associates allegedly attacked Idris Ali’s house with locally made weapons.

The case statement alleges that the attackers damaged the walls, doors and windows, tin roof and furniture of Idris Ali’s house, causing losses worth around Tk 250,000. When Idris Ali tried to stop them, he and his wife, Mina Khatun, were beaten with sticks.

The attackers also allegedly looted three beds and 10 bundles of tin sheets, along with other belongings worth around Tk 150,000.

In his case statement, Idris Ali further said that when he sought justice from local residents after the incident, Abdul Halim instead filed a case against him at Daulatpur Police Station on 16 September last year. He had to serve time in jail in connection with that case.

After securing bail, he learnt that Abdul Halim has taken possession of the land by using the influence of his daughter, MP Nusrat Tabassum. When Idris Ali protested, he was threatened with being implicated in an arms case. As a result, he left the area with his family and took shelter at his in-law’s house.

The case statement also says that a fire broke out at Abdul Halim’s house on 12 November. Idris Ali said he has learnt that attempts were being made to falsely implicate him and his family members in a case filed over that incident.

Will be doubtful of probe’s impartiality after home minister’s remarks: Nusrat Tabassum

Fearing this, he filed the complaint at the police station. He stated that fear, intimidation and concerns for his safety had prevented him from filing a case earlier over the alleged attack, states the case statement.

When contacted, case plaintiff Idris Ali told Prothom Alo, “I bought the land from Abdul Halim’s brothers. The land I purchased is near the bamboo grove below Halim’s house. I filed a case at the police station over last year’s incident.”

Nusrat’s father knows nothing about the case

Asked about the allegations in the case, Abdul Halim, the father of MP Nusrat, told Prothom Alo, “I know nothing about the case. Idris Ali does not live in the area. He has disputes with many people in the area. As far as I know, he has been absconding since 5 August 2024.”

Abdul Halim added, “There was an issue concerning the purchase and sale of my brothers’ land. Perhaps someone instigated Idris Ali to file the case now. I know nothing about it yet.”

item.title: Man caught up in arms case for 22 years because of namesake, fails to travel to Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Mohammad Almas of Dohar, Dhaka, has been caught up in an arms case for 22 years because of a namesake. After being detained twice in 2004 and 2018, he was arrested on 4 November 2025. He returned home on 10 November after spending a year in prison. Azharul Haque listened to the long story of his ordeal.

I had just returned home after work and taken my daughter into my arms 4 November 2025. At that moment, the police arrived in the yard to arrest me. I knew it was that old arms case. I showed the police the previous documents. The people around also came forward, saying that I was not the accused in that case.

But the police did not listen to anyone. They handcuffed me and took me to the outpost. After spending a night at the Dohar police station, I was sent to the central jail.

Inside, I was shattered. I couldn't eat. I would lie down, thinking why, despite committing no crime or injustice, I had to remain in jail month after month! I would cry. Other inmates would console me, offering comfort. During this time, I missed my daughter's face the most.

What happened

In 2004, I was about 10 or 12 years old. One day, I was returning home with cattle from the field when the police stopped me and took me into custody. People from the area protested at the police station after hearing the news. Later, I was released.

In 2018, I was detained again. At that time, I realised that due to a name match, I was being sought as an accused in someone else's case. I learned that an arms case was filed on 10 April 2002, at the Mirpur police station in Dhaka. The accused was Almas Hossain, son of Khaleel Ahmed from South Bahra village. He was sentenced to 10 years. After being released on bail, he went abroad. But due to the similarity in his name and his father's name with mine, I got into trouble.

My name is Md. Almas, and my father’s name is Sheikh Khaleel. The accused's name is Almas Hossain, and his father's name is Khaleel Ahmed.

Even the addresses are almost the same

Despite the names being nearly identical, we are different people. To prove this, I took a certificate from the then-chairman of our union, Amzad Hossain Azad. The chairman of Kusumhati union Parishad, Abdul Wahab Dohari, also gave me a certificate. Those certificates stated that I was not the accused in that case.

I have never lived in Dhaka. I don't even know Mirpur. Yet my name and address came up as the accused in the case. My mother’s name is Rashnara/Rasara Begum, while the real accused Almas Hossain's mother’s name is Salma Akhtar. Had these details been verified, maybe I wouldn’t have faced such a situation, or endured this harassment for so long.

I got married in 2017. Initially, my wife (Bannya Akhtar) didn't know about the hassle of this case. She found out after I was detained again in 2018. Since then, alongside the joys and sorrows of family life, she had to handle this legal complication with me.

After 2018, I thought maybe I would be free from this hassle this time. I had taken certificates from the chairmen and revealed my identity. After that, the police didn't come to the house. I didn’t have to attend court hearings either. So, gradually, I tried to settle into a normal life. I learned to work at an electrician's shop in Kartikpur Bazar. Gradually, I started supporting the family by doing electric work.

Since 2018, I also tried to go abroad. In 2025, I even got a visa for Saudi Arabia. For that, I had deposited 4. 5 lakh taka. I had arranged this money by taking loans. But before going abroad, I was arrested.

Who will compensate?

While in jail, one day some inmates called me over and said there was news about me in the newspaper. From them, I learned that a report on my case was done by the Prothom Alo. I’m not very educated, having studied up to the third grade. Others read the report aloud to me. Hearing the news, I felt like maybe there would be progress this time. Maybe I would get justice and be free.

Family members also went to court for my release. On 8 November, the High Court ordered my swift release. I was released from Dhaka's Keraniganj Central Jail on 10 November. I returned home after a year. Relatives and neighbors came. There were smiles on my wife and children's faces. But this past year, my wife had to endure a lot. She had to look after one son, one daughter, and her elderly in-laws. Even after hearing about the release order, she waited at the jail gate for two days.

Indeed, I have come back from jail, but I can't focus on work as before. Neither my body nor my mind is the same. I keep recalling the days spent in jail without being guilty. I feel like 12 months have taken over 12 years of my life.

While imprisoned, my Saudi visa got canceled as well. The money has become a burden of debt. I hope the government seeks a fair trial for the loss in my life.

Why was I harassed for so many years for a crime I didn’t commit? Why did I have to spend a year in jail? Why do I have to start a new life under the weight of debt?

The lost time over 22 years, broken dreams, and the suffering of my family cannot be regained. Now I only want justice for the damage in my life.

item.title: A family, a fire and a photograph: How Pinu Rahman won a Tk 25 million prize
item.description:
A family sleeps in a room gutted by fire. Despite losing everything, the family’s bond and love for one another remain unbroken. For capturing this poignant humanitarian message in a photograph, Bangladeshi photographer Pinu Rahman has won the grand prize at the Hamdan International Photography Award (HIPA). The United Arab Emirates-based award carries prize money of USD 200,000, or nearly Tk 25 million. He shares the story behind the photograph with Prothom Alo’s Sozib Mia.

A fire broke out at Korail slum in the capital on 25 November 2025. It was a Tuesday. I work as a banker, and because I had to go to the office that day, I could not visit the scene. This happens quite often. I decided that I would photograph the aftermath of the fire.

In similar incidents in the past, I have mostly taken photographs of the situation after the event. Two of my younger friends, who are also photographers and were outside Dhaka, called and said they also wanted to go there to take photographs.

We planned to go together on Friday, 28 November. The plan was to meet at Karwan Bazar and travel to the site together. But I left home very early, so in the end we could not go together. I reached the scene at around 5:30 or 6:00 am.

I initially took some photographs with my camera. At the same time, I kept looking for my friends, but I could not find them. Meanwhile, I noticed many drones flying in the sky.

Pinu Rahman wins grand prize at HIPA

It was impossible to cover such a large area on foot. So I went up to the roof of a nearby single-storey building and flew my own drone. For about 30 minutes, I used it to survey the situation across the entire area. None of the houses in the fire-ravaged section had any tin roofing left. The burnt sheets of tin were scattered all around.

People who had lost their homes were sleeping under the open sky, some under mosquito nets and others without them. Some had put up tarpaulins for shelter. Others had woken up. Some were having breakfast, while others were talking on their phones. I captured these scenes with my drone and returned home.

The photo of the five family members sleeping struck me differently. They looked utterly exhausted. Perhaps they would wake up after a little while.

Story of a ‘family’ in the photo

I downloaded the photographs onto my computer and sat down to look through them. As I went through the images, a few frames caught my eye. In one, five members of a family were sleeping side by side. In another, a different family is sitting together having breakfast; some are chatting while another is talking on the phone. Just, moments from everyday life.

But the photo of the five family members sleeping struck me differently. They looked utterly exhausted. Perhaps they would wake up after a little while.

I sent the photographs to an international news organisation. It selected 20 of them. The organisation’s chief executive, on seeing the photograph of the sleeping family, said there were many stories within the image and that I should save the photo carefully.

I, too, had a similar feeling about the photograph. So I kept it aside.

Under the same sky

Every year, the Hamdan International Photography Award (HIPA) sets a specific theme for its competition. Last year’s theme was ‘Power’, while the year before that it was ‘Sustainability’. This year, the theme was ‘Family’.

I read the explanation of the theme on HIPA’s website. Family was not limited to relationships between people. There was also scope to explore the idea of family in nature. The main aim of this year’s theme was to highlight connections, a sense of togetherness and bonds.

I began thinking about various photographs, trying to work out which one best matched the theme. From my years of experience in photography, I know that understanding the theme is essential when submitting photographs to international competitions. It is not enough for a photograph to be beautiful, it must also fit the spirit of the competition.

JAC photo contest winners awarded

At one point, I remembered the photograph from Korail slum. Even after their homes had been gutted by fire, five members of a family were sleeping together. They had been left without shelter, a home or possessions, yet they were still together. The family bond, even in the face of disaster, was the photograph’s greatest strength.

Fires in slums are nothing new. Though regrettable, the reality is that such incidents occur somewhere or other every year. Yet people pick themselves up and try to rebuild their lives. I also saw in the photograph the struggle of people rising from the ruins, like the mythical phoenix.

After considering everything, I decided to submit the photograph. I titled it ‘Under the Same Sky’. I also wrote down my thoughts in the description.

First came the third prize, followed by the second, but my name was not called. Then the first prize was announced. My name was not there either. I was a little surprised. Was I not going to win any award at all?

A surprise at the awards ceremony

I had received some indication from HIPA that I would be getting an award, but they had not told me which one. At their invitation, I set off on 9 November with my wife and Prothom Alo’s chief photographer, Zahidul Islam, to attend the awards ceremony.

On the morning of 10 November, a rehearsal was held for the winners in the various categories. We were shown how to walk onto the stage, receive the awards and complete the formalities. Even after the nearly two-hour rehearsal, we still did not know who had won first, second or third place.

The main ceremony began in the afternoon. Members of the royal family and various other dignitaries were among those present. Before the ceremony, several people came over to speak to me in particular. Seeing this, Zahidul Bhai said, “Pinu, it looks as if something big is waiting for you.”

I replied, “I hope I’ll at least win third prize!”

Then the awards were announced. First came the third prize, followed by the second, but my name was not called. Then the first prize was announced. My name was not there either. I was a little surprised. Was I not going to win any award at all?

Finally, the grand prize was announced. The presenter said that this year’s grand prize had gone to a photograph from Bangladesh. The photographer’s name was Pinu Rahman.

The photograph that had stood out to me from the very first time I saw it, had brought me international recognition. Now it is time to find the family in the picture. It will not be easy, but I have a few plans.

item.title: Started up with Tk 90,000, now worth millions
item.description:
Entrepreneur Nitai Sarkar once ran a mobile phone top-up shop. He later bought clothes and bedsheets from wholesale markets and sold them online. Eventually, he began manufacturing bedsheets and other home decor products himself. Through gradual expansion of his own production and online marketing operations, he built a home decor brand called ‘Ortha’.

Nitai Sarkar’s interest in business began in childhood. It started as a hobby when he sold chanachur, the popular spicy snack mix, and apples at religious festival events. That childhood interest eventually turned him into an entrepreneur. He worked for three years after completing his undergraduate degree, and then eventually decided to venture into business.

Nitai Sarkar’s company, Ortha, now manufactures and sells a range of home decor products, including bedsheets, pillows, pillowcases, curtains, mosquito nets and duvets. The company began its journey nearly 12 years ago. It currently employs 21 people and generates annual revenue of more than Tk 1 crore (Tk 10 million).

Last Tuesday, we spoke with Ortha founder Nitai Sarkar at his office in Paikpara, Mirpur-1. During the conversation, he shared stories from the various stages of his entrepreneurial journey.

Nitai Sarkar’s ancestral home is in Ghagra village, Kachua upazila, Chandpur. His father was a government employee, while his mother was a primary school teacher. After completing his secondary education locally and higher secondary education at Cumilla Government College, he earned a Bachelor of Business Administration (BBA) degree in Marketing from Eastern University in Dhaka in 2012.

Nitai Sarkar said his first major challenge after completing his BBA was securing an internship. With no personal connections or professional network in Dhaka, he struggled to find an opportunity despite trying for six months. Rather than remain idle during this period, he started a mobile phone top-up business next to his uncle’s pharmacy in Old Dhaka. Later, with the help of a university teacher, he secured an internship at Fortuna Bangladesh, a footwear company. He subsequently worked at the company for nearly three years.

His responsibilities at Fortuna were not limited to any particular department. He handled almost everything, including collecting customer feedback, product photography, inventory management, supply chain operations, managing the company’s Facebook page, product deliveries and participating in various trade fairs. The experience gave him hands-on knowledge of how an e-commerce business operates on a day-to-day basis.

He later used that experience as the foundation for his own business. “While working at Fortuna, I didn’t just learn how to sell products; I became familiar with the different aspects of running a business from beginning to end,” he said. Moreover, participating in various trade fairs helped him build an extensive network, many members of which later became his customers.

Starting with online sales

He left his job and ventured into business in late 2015. Initially, he planned to work in event management. Even before that, in late 2014, he had created a Facebook page called ‘Ortha’. However, things did not go according to plan.

During this period, Nitai Sarkar became involved in various activities of the e-Commerce Association of Bangladesh (e-CAB), where he expanded his network of fellow entrepreneurs. This exposure inspired him to start selling different products online.

He initially began selling jewellery by posting product photos on Ortha’s Facebook page. He collected pictures from various shops and business owners and posted them on Facebook. Whenever he received an order, he would collect the product from the supplier and deliver it to the customer.

Through this approach, he generated sales of approximately Tk 16 lakh (Tk 1.6 million) in 2016 from various products, with three-piece outfits accounting for the bulk of the sales. He also began selling bedsheets and pillowcases online.

Focus on bed linen

One of Nitai’s well-wishers told him that the three-piece clothing market was highly competitive, but there was an opportunity to build a specialised brand around products such as eight-piece bed sheet sets. Taking this advice, Nitai decided to give up selling three-piece outfits and focus exclusively on bed linen. This decision changed the course of his business.

Initially, he sourced fabric from Islampur in the capital and had bedsheets made by tailors. He then sold them online. In 2017, he rented a room in Paikpara, Mirpur, installed sewing machines and hired a skilled craftsman.

During difficult periods in his business journey, his mother's words repeatedly gave him the courage to carry on: “Never cheat anyone, and you will never be cheated yourself.”

At the time, his initial investment was approximately Tk 90,000, covering the cost of machinery, room rent, advance payment and other expenses.

As the business expanded, so did its capital requirements. Securing his first loan proved quite difficult. The lack of necessary documents and a guarantor posed major obstacles. According to Nitai, accessing financial institutions and preparing the required documentation are major challenges for new entrepreneurs.

His business currently has a total investment of more than Tk 50 lakh (Tk 5 million), of which approximately Tk 32 lakh (Tk 3.2 million) comes from bank loans.

'Ortha' today

Ortha’s main products currently include bedsheets, pillows, curtains, mosquito nets and duvets. According to Nitai, bedsheets account for approximately 70 per cent of the company’s total business, while the remaining 30 per cent comes from other products. Last winter, the company sold around 10,000 duvets. So far, Ortha has sold its products to more than 100,000 customers. In addition to a small factory in Mirpur, the company also operates a showroom and an office.

Ortha’s bedsheets and duvets are priced between Tk 1,000 and Tk 3,500 each. Mosquito nets sell for Tk 500 to Tk 1,200, while curtains are priced between Tk 500 and Tk 3,500 per piece.

The company serves a diverse customer base, ranging from walk-in showroom customers to online shoppers and visitors at trade fairs. Its products are also supplied to various hotels and resorts, hospitals and corporate organisations. However, approximately 80 per cent of Ortha’s total sales come from online channels.

However, he now wants to reduce the company’s dependence on online sales and expand its showroom network. He also plans to introduce new products, including items made by combining jute and fabric. For Nitai Sarkar, business is not just about selling products and making profits; building long-term relationships with customers is equally important. That is why he reinvests a portion of his profits in initiatives for customers.

Nitai Sarkar believes that while people are conscious about the quality of their clothing and food, they pay comparatively less attention to their sleeping environment. Yet people spend nearly eight hours a day in bed. Therefore, he believes that fabric quality and comfort should be given greater consideration when choosing bedroom products. Accordingly, Ortha places particular emphasis on fabric, stitching and accurate measurements to ensure product quality.

During difficult periods in his business journey, his mother's words repeatedly gave him the courage to carry on: “Never cheat anyone, and you will never be cheated yourself.”

For him, this advice from his mother is more than just an emotional reassurance; it is also a source of strength that continues to inspire him as an entrepreneur.

item.title: Bhutan’s fate unchanged after 18 years as India reach final
item.description:
The year was 2008. In the SAFF Championship semi-final in Male, Bhutan lost 2–1 to India, missing out on a place in the final. Eighteen years later, the two sides met again in the last four of the tournament.

Time has passed and the competition has moved to a different level, but the result remained unchanged. India once again secured a 2–1 victory to reach the final, while Bhutan suffered another semi-final exit.

India booked their place in the final by beating Bhutan in the first semi-final at Dhaka’s National Stadium today, Saturday. Although India came to this edition with a second-string side, they have continued their march towards the title.

India’s dominance in the SAFF Championship is nothing new. Including this edition, they have participated in the tournament 15 times and reached the final on 14 occasions.

They have won the title nine times and finished runners-up four times. Their only other finish was third place in 2003. In 2009, they also won the championship in Bangladesh with an Olympic team.

SAFF Championship: Bangladesh face Pakistan in semifinal today

India started aggressively against Bhutan today. They took the lead in the ninth minute through a goal by Bishnu. Defender Chinglensana Singh doubled the advantage in the 28th minute. Conceding two early goals put Bhutan under considerable pressure. They subsequently focused more on attacking but failed to break through India's solid defence in the first half.

Bhutan managed just one shot on target from three attempts in the first 45 minutes. India, meanwhile, had four shots, three of which were on target. India were clearly superior in both possession and attacking play in the first half.

Bhutan, however, attempted to fight back after the break. They scored just two minutes into the second half. In the 47th minute, Chencho's shot came back off the post, and Kinzaang Tashi headed the rebound into the net.

Referee Munir Alkatiri initially ruled the goal out for offside. However, following protests from Bhutan's players, he turned to VAR. After reviewing the footage, the referee overturned his initial decision and awarded the goal.

Bangladesh thrash Sri Lanka 4-0 to top group in SAFF Championship

Video Assistant Referee (VAR) technology is being used for the first time in SAFF Championship history. The technology is available for both semi-finals and the final. In the 66th minute, the referee awarded Bhutan a penalty against India, but the decision was overturned following a VAR review.

After reducing the deficit to 2–1, Bhutan grew increasingly desperate to find an equaliser. They created several good opportunities in the final half-hour but could not find the goal they needed. India eventually walked off with a 2–1 victory.
